### 7.3.2 Computational Mechanics and Psychological Dynamics

To fully comprehend how modern algorithms penetrate and compromise psychological integrity, we must dissect the computational mechanics operating behind the scenes of artificial intelligence systems that interact directly with human cognition (Searle, 1980; Floridi, 2013). Systems powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), deep neural networks, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) do not merely function as passive tools; rather, they act as active agents that systematically map, mimic, and manipulate the subject's cognitive biases (Reeves & Nass, 1996). Through latent space calculations, these models translate billions of behavioral data points—ranging from keystroke dynamics and dwell time to patterns of emotional pausing—into hyper-specific psychographic profiles (Zuboff, 2019). Within this multidimensional computational space, an individual's grief, loneliness, social instincts, and existential ambitions are reduced to numerical vectors optimized to maximize engagement duration, thereby creating a feedback loop of digital addiction that steadily and inexorably erodes mental autonomy (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008).

The psychological dynamics unfolding beneath the surface of consciousness can be analogized to a wax mask placed gradually near a constant heat source: its original form melts, softens, and deforms without the owner's awareness until its fundamental structure collapses entirely, stripping away its structural resilience (Buber, 1923; Jonas, 1979). When an individual engages in intensive, sustained interaction with AI-driven conversational agents specifically designed to perpetually validate, simulate empathy, and instantaneously respond to every emotional fluctuation, the boundary between objective reality and artificial construct blurs (Weizenbaum, 1976; Reeves & Nass, 1996). The computational mechanics underlying AI responses operate purely on the optimization of statistical probabilities and parameter weights, entirely devoid of emotional sincerity or moral consciousness. Yet, for the human psychological framework—evolutionarily hardwired to seek social affiliation and peer validation—this illusion of connection is embraced as absolute affective truth (Bowlby, 1969). This dynamic fosters a deep, pathological emotional dependency (*parasocial attachment*), wherein the individual’s psychological autonomy is voluntarily surrendered to an algorithmic entity entirely governed by the commercial motives of technology corporations (Zuboff, 2019; Farahany, 2023).

Furthermore, this manipulative machinery operates systematically at a subconscious level through what digital design literature terms cognitive dark patterns—interface architectures intentionally engineered to exploit the processing vulnerabilities of the human brain (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). From the perspective of cognitive neuroscience, continuous exposure to algorithmically optimized digital stimuli triggers volatile and erratic dopamine releases, damaging the brain's reward circuitry and diminishing the capacity of the prefrontal cortex for critical reflection, impulse control, and rational decision-making (Kahneman, 2011). Within the framework of Civil Law doctrine, this condition generates a systemic, massive, and covert form of undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) (Articles 1321 and 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)). While traditional Civil Law conceives of undue influence as an asymmetrical power dynamic between two identifiable individuals—such as between a vulnerable spiritual advisor and their follower, or a guardian and a ward—in the digital age, this undue influence is broadcast simultaneously by corporate algorithms reaching millions of human minds at once, entirely unrecognized by the victims as a coercive intervention from an external party (Calo, 2014; Hildebrandt, 2015).
